outcome: Since 26 January 2024 I found no source that enumerates, classifies or proves complete the convex uniform 5-polytopes; the current Wikipedia article and the Polytope Wiki still say the complete set is not known, and the only in-window change to a count of known 5-polytopes is an April 2024 Wikipedia edit naming a polytope ('snub cellibiprismatoteron') that I could not identify.
problem_asks: (a) Find the complete set of convex uniform 5-polytopes: every convex 5-polytope that is vertex-transitive with all facets uniform 4-polytopes, including the infinite families of prismatic and duoprism-type members the Wikipedia entry counts separately. (b) Classify that set, i.e. sort its members into their families and construction classes (Wythoffian constructions from the A5, B5 and D5 symmetry groups, prismatic products, and any non-Wythoffian members). (c) Establish that the list is complete, i.e. that no convex uniform 5-polytope lies outside it. The statement as frozen asks for 'the complete set'; Wikipedia's unsolved-problem box words it as 'What is the complete set of convex uniform 5-polytopes?'. Non-convex uniform 5-polytopes are not asked for.

events.what_happened: Ludwig Schlafli's treatise 'Theorie der vielfachen Kontinuitat' (manuscript 1850-52; full text first published 1901, edited by J. H. Graf, Neue Denkschriften der Schweizerischen Naturforschenden Gesellschaft) classifies the regular polytopes. The Wikipedia article (fetched) states that he proved there are exactly 3 regular polytopes in 5 or more dimensions, which in dimension 5 are the 5-simplex, 5-cube and 5-orthoplex. Date given is the first full publication. Earlier partial publications (Crelle, Liouville, Quarterly Journal; Cayley's English portions of 1860) exist, and I did not check whether any carries the 5-dimensional material.
events.revisions: Manuscript 1850-52 (Wikipedia gives 1852 as the original year); full publication 1901.
events.delivers: Classifies the regular convex 5-polytopes: exactly three (5-simplex, 5-cube, 5-orthoplex). Restricted to regular polytopes, so it says nothing about non-regular uniform members.
events.remains: All non-regular convex uniform 5-polytopes; the enumeration of the uniform (non-regular) members; completeness of the full convex list.
events.directly_checkable: The three regular 5-polytopes are the standard simplex, hypercube and cross-polytope, checkable from their definitions; not re-checked in this run.
events.doubts: The 1901 text was not opened and no verification statement for it was read in this run.
events.direction: Cuts toward the regular subclass: three members in dimension 5, which are all in the convex uniform list.
people: J. H. Graf (editor of the 1901 edition)

events.what_happened: Thorold Gosset, 'On the Regular and Semi-Regular Figures in Space of n Dimensions' (Messenger of Mathematics, 1900), enumerates the nonprismatic semiregular convex polytopes with regular facets, listed without a completeness argument (Wikipedia, fetched, footnote 1). The list includes the 5-dimensional semiregular polytope, the demipenteract (1_21); the Wikipedia 5-polytope article's semiregular note (from a search summary of the article, not the fetched text) says there is only one semiregular 5-polytope.
events.delivers: Lists the semiregular convex 5-polytope (demipenteract) and the higher-dimensional k21 family as members of the semiregular list, without proof of completeness. Restricted to semiregular polytopes (uniform, with regular facets of at least two types).
events.remains: Every uniform convex 5-polytope that is not semiregular; the completeness of the semiregular list itself, which was not proved until 1991 (see blind-blind-1991-semiregular-completeness).
events.doubts: The list was given without proof. One search summary gives 1899 for the discovery and 1900 for publication; I did not open Gosset's paper to settle this.
events.direction: Partial enumeration of a subclass; it lists one 5-dimensional member and asserts no completeness, so it does not settle the convex question.

events.what_happened: H. S. M. Coxeter, 'Regular and semi-regular polytopes I' (Math. Z. 46, 1940, pp. 380-407), with Parts II and III to 1988. The Wikipedia article (fetched) says the search for uniform polytopes was 'expanded systematically' by Coxeter in this series, and that most known convex uniform 5-polytopes come from Wythoff constructions. I read only these summaries, not the papers.
events.revisions: Part I 1940; Parts II and III later, with the series dated 1940-1988 by secondary sources.
events.delivers: A systematic Wythoffian (Coxeter-Wythoff construction) search for uniform polytopes in dimensions 5 and up, as described by secondary sources. None of the sources I opened says the 5-dimensional list was shown complete; the Wikipedia article (current) says the complete set has not been determined.
events.remains: Completeness of the convex 5-dimensional list; any non-Wythoffian members beyond the grand antiprism prism, which Wikipedia states is the only non-Wythoffian member among the known convex 5-polytopes.
events.doubts: What Parts I-III establish for dimension 5 was not read. A search summary says the sources do not show whether the 1940 paper included a completeness argument. Whether Coxeter meant the search to be exhaustive in dimension 5 is therefore unverified; I read it as not exhaustive because the sources I opened say the list is not known to be complete.
events.direction: Cuts toward a construction-based enumeration of Wythoffian members, which by the sources' own account does not exhaust the convex list.

events.what_happened: Norman W. Johnson, 'The Theory of Uniform Polytopes and Honeycombs', PhD dissertation, University of Toronto, 1966, under Coxeter. The Wikipedia article (fetched) says it describes two non-convex uniform antiprisms in 5-space. Johnson's Uniform Polytopes manuscript (1991, unpublished) is cited but its contents page reads 'Contents coming...' on the roice3 host. The dissertation itself was not opened.
events.delivers: Two non-convex uniform 5-dimensional antiprisms, per Wikipedia. Restricted to non-convex members, so it does not bear on the convex list.
events.doubts: The non-convex claim comes from the Wikipedia summary; the dissertation was not read.
events.direction: Non-convex examples; discarded for scope against the convex question.
events.object: Two non-convex uniform antiprisms in 5-space, per Wikipedia citing the dissertation. They are not explicit in any source I read; the descriptions were not checked, and they are non-convex, so they are not members of the convex list.

events.what_happened: J. H. Conway and M. J. T. Guy, 'Four-dimensional Archimedean polytopes' (presented at the Copenhagen Colloquium on Convexity, 1965; proceedings 1967), a computer analysis giving the convex uniform 4-polytopes. It adds the grand antiprism (4D) as the only non-Wythoffian convex 4-polytope. Johnson's own site (fetched) says Conway and Guy proved the list of uniform 4-polytopes complete in 1965. The 5-dimensional relevance: the Wikipedia 5-polytope article (fetched) states that all known convex uniform 5-polytopes except the grand antiprism prism are Wythoffian, so the 5-dimensional prism over the grand antiprism is a known non-Wythoffian convex member.
events.revisions: Presented 1965 (Copenhagen); published proceedings 1967 (per a search summary). The write-up is dated here, following the rule that a talk is dated to its written version.
events.delivers: For dimension 4: a computer enumeration of the convex uniform 4-polytopes, claimed complete (per Johnson's site and Wikipedia-derived pages). For dimension 5: one known non-Wythoffian convex member, the grand antiprism prism, by prismatic extension of the 4D object. Restricted to dimension 4 except for that prism.
events.remains: Whether the 5-dimensional convex list is complete; whether any non-Wythoffian 5-dimensional members exist beyond the prism.

checked_by.who: Marco Moller, 'Vierdimensionale Archimedische Polytope' (2004 dissertation, see moller-2004-4d-completeness-claim)
checked_by.qualification: Doctoral candidate at Universitat Hamburg (Mathematics Genealogy Project record; advisors A. Kreuzer and R. Frank)
checked_by.what_they_did: Per secondary sources, the dissertation proves that the Conway-Guy list is complete; I did not open the text

events.directly_checkable: The 4D grand antiprism can be generated from its vertex set (100 vertices; 20 pentagonal antiprisms and 300 regular tetrahedra as cells, per search summaries). Not constructed in this run.
events.doubts: Counts of nonprismatic convex forms differ across secondary sources (44, 45, 47 and 64 appear). Coxeter's symmetry group [[10,2+,10]] for the grand antiprism is disputed by Monson (2024). Whether the 1965 work was itself a proof, or a computation completed by a later proof, is disputed in the sources.
events.direction: For dimension 4 it confirms a complete convex list; for dimension 5 it supplies a known non-Wythoffian member by prism, which cuts toward the existence of members outside the Wythoffian families but says nothing on completeness in dimension 5.
events.object: The grand antiprism (4D, found by Conway and Guy by computer): 100 vertices, bounded by 20 pentagonal antiprisms and 300 regular tetrahedra, two rings of ten antiprisms in orthogonal planes with tetrahedra filling the space between them (per search summaries). It is explicit (computer-found vertex set), not a non-constructive existence result. The 5-dimensional object is the prism over it, which Wikipedia calls the grand antiprism prism and says is non-Wythoffian. Its symmetry group is disputed (see disputes).

events.what_happened: Marco Moller, 'Vierdimensionale Archimedische Polytope', Dissertation, Universitat Hamburg (oral examination 12 July 2004; advisor A. Kreuzer). Secondary sources (Wikipedia-derived copies found by search) say it proves that the Conway-Guy list of convex uniform 4-polytopes is complete. The bibliographic record was read from the Hamburg repository listing; the PDF (handle ediss/689) was not opened.
events.delivers: Claimed completeness of the convex uniform 4-polytope list (per secondary sources). Restricted by its title to dimension 4; it claims nothing about dimension 5 as far as I could tell.
events.doubts: The completeness claim comes only from secondary summaries; the text was not read, so I cannot say whether the argument covers all cases. Whether any later reviewer engaged with it was not established.
events.direction: Analogue in dimension 4; it cuts toward a complete list in 4D, not toward the 5-dimensional question.

events.what_happened: Gerd Blind and Roswitha Blind, 'The semiregular polytopes', Commentarii Mathematici Helvetici 66 (1991), 150-154, prove the completeness of Gosset's list of semiregular polytopes. Known only from secondary summaries (a German-language search summary citing Wikipedia-derived pages); the paper was not opened. The same summaries credit Makarov (1988) with the 4-dimensional case.
events.delivers: Completeness of the semiregular list, in all dimensions. In dimension 5 this is the single semiregular member (the demipenteract). Restricted to the semiregular class; it settles that subclass only.
events.remains: Every uniform convex 5-polytope that is not semiregular, which is most of the known list (the A5, B5 and D5 Wythoffian families and the prismatic families).

checked_by.qualification: Researchers on homogeneous and semiregular polytopes (Izvestiya paper; arXiv 2304.12211)
checked_by.what_they_did: Use the Gosset/semiregular list as input to a classification of perfect polytopes; the abstract I read does not say they re-verified the Blind-Blind proof. A search summary says a 2021 Izvestiya paper credits G. and R. Blind with the proof; not opened.

events.doubts: Primary paper not opened; completeness is from secondary summaries. The date of the Gosset list is given as 1899 or 1900 depending on source.
events.direction: Cuts toward completeness for the semiregular subclass; it has no bearing on the non-semiregular members.

events.what_happened: Open Problem Garden entry 'Enumerate all convex uniform 5-polytopes', posted 24 May 2012 by ACW (subject Geometry; importance medium; no comments shown). It is a status record, not a result: it reports two infinite families plus 105 additional examples, says almost all are Wythoffian, and says any undiscovered example must be non-Wythoffian.
events.delivers: No new result. States the 2012 state of knowledge: two infinite families plus 105 additional convex examples.
events.doubts: The 105 count does not match the 104 given in the current Wikipedia article (see disputes); the counting conventions are not stated in either source.
events.direction: Problem statement with a 2012 status; it expects non-Wythoffian members if any remain.
people: ACW (poster on the Open Problem Garden)

events.what_happened: Spencer Whitehead, 'Classifying Regular Polyhedra and Polytopes using Wythoff's Construction', arXiv:2001.09364, first submitted 25 January 2020, revised December 2021. It uses Coxeter diagrams with crosses to classify regular polytopes and gives an alternative proof of Schlafli's classification. Regular polytopes only.
events.revisions: v1 25 Jan 2020; revised December 2021 (more proofs, definitions fixed), per the arXiv listing and a search summary.
events.delivers: Alternative proof of the regular polytope classification, which includes the three regular 5-polytopes. Restricted to regular polytopes.
events.direction: Regular subclass only; reproves rather than extends Schlafli's result, so it cuts neither way on the convex list.

events.what_happened: V. N. Berestovskii and Yu. G. Nikonorov, 'Perfect and almost perfect homogeneous polytopes', arXiv:2304.12211, submitted 24 April 2023 (v1 only). They classify perfect and almost perfect polytopes among the regular and semiregular polytopes, excepting the Archimedean solids and two 4-dimensional Gosset polytopes, and construct some non-regular homogeneous polytopes. The abstract does not use the word 'uniform' and does not enumerate uniform 5-polytopes.
events.revisions: v1 only, per the arXiv page.
events.delivers: Classifies perfect and almost perfect members of the regular and semiregular classes, with the stated exceptions. A metric property of the polytopes, not membership in the uniform list.
events.remains: The whole problem as stated: the complete list of convex uniform 5-polytopes.
events.direction: A different question (perfectness), which neither confirms nor contradicts the convex list.

events.what_happened: Barry Monson, 'The Symmetry Group of the Grand Antiprism', posted on Preprints.org (submitted 1 August 2024, posted 2 August 2024, ID 202408.0116) and published in Symmetry 16(8), 1071 (2024), per a bibliographic record. It argues that the symmetry group G(A) of the 4-dimensional grand antiprism is the group +/-[D10 x D10].2 of order 400, not Coxeter's [[10,2+,10]]. Both Preprints.org and MDPI returned HTTP 403 to my fetches; the content is known only from search summaries.
events.revisions: Preprints.org v1, 2 Aug 2024; journal version Symmetry 2024, 16(8), 1071.
events.delivers: A correction to the symmetry group of the 4D grand antiprism, which the summaries say is the only uniform 4-polytope not obtainable by Wythoff's construction. Restricted to the 4D object; the 5-dimensional prism over it inherits the object but the summaries do not say whether its symmetry is discussed.

checked_by.what_they_did: Published the article (per a bibliographic record; the article page itself returned 403 and was not read)

events.doubts: Not read: the preprint and journal article both refused fetches. The claim is Monson's own, and the search summaries report that a 2023 conference abstract by the same author had already raised the ambiguity.
events.direction: A 4D correction that cuts neither way on the 5-dimensional completeness question.

events.what_happened: Bruno Martelli, 'An introduction to Coxeter polyhedra', arXiv:2601.07552 (v1 12 Jan 2026; v2 16 Jan 2026; v3 1 May 2026). It introduces non-obtuse polyhedra in spherical, Euclidean and hyperbolic space and uses them to describe regular, semiregular and uniform polyhedra and tessellations, mostly via the Wythoff construction. I read the abstract, the introduction, Sections 1-4 and part of Section 5 (to 5.6.2); the PDF exceeded the fetch size limit, so Sections 5.7-5.13 and the references were not read. The text read contains no mention of 5-polytopes or of an enumeration of uniform 5-polytopes.
events.revisions: v1 12 Jan 2026; v2 16 Jan 2026; v3 1 May 2026 (current).
events.delivers: A general framework and background on Coxeter and Wythoff polyhedra and tessellations, with classification statements for 3D polyhedra and simplices. Nothing on the 5-dimensional convex list in the text read.
events.direction: Neighbouring framework on polyhedra and tessellations; no bearing on the 5-dimensional question in the text I could read.

events.what_happened: Egon Schulte and Tomas Skacel, 'Skeletal Snub Polyhedra in Ordinary Space, I', arXiv:2602.19391, submitted 22 February 2026 (v1 only). A snub construction on regular and chiral skeletal polyhedra in 3D space, with a discussion of when it yields uniform skeletal polyhedra and of the completeness of the generated list. Abstract only.
events.delivers: Snub constructions on 3D skeletal polyhedra. Restricted to 3D skeletal polyhedra; no 5-polytope content in the abstract.
events.direction: Different dimension and object; discarded for scope.

events.what_happened: Grzegorz Swirszcz, Adam Zsolt Wagner, Geordie Williamson, Sam Blackwell, Bogdan Georgiev, Alex Davies, Ali Eslami, Sebastien Racaniere, Theophane Weber and Pushmeet Kohli, 'Advancing Geometry with AI: Multi-agent Generation of Polytopes', arXiv:2502.05199 (math.CO; submitted 30 January 2025, v1 only). The paper presents an AI search ('Hopper') that generates polytopes for the Hirsch conjecture, the k-neighbourly problem and the longest monotone path problem, and reports over a million 5-dimensional prismatoids of width 6 and a 24-vertex example. It does not describe any generated polytope as uniform, and it does not address the uniform 5-polytope list.
events.revisions: v1 only (30 Jan 2025), per the arXiv page.
events.delivers: Polytopes for other problems (Hirsch conjecture, k-neighbourly, monotone paths) and non-uniform 5-dimensional prismatoids. Restricted to those objects; nothing on uniform or convex-uniform 5-polytopes.
events.doubts: The abstract's claims that the examples match or beat best known bounds are the authors' and were not checked. A search summary reports a 19-dimensional Hirsch counterexample; I did not confirm that figure in the paper.
events.direction: Cuts neither way on the uniform 5-polytope question; it concerns a different set of problems.

systems.name: Hopper algorithm (the authors' own; no named model)
systems.what_it_did: A population search in which a transformer-based network scores hyperplanes to move polytope vertices, generating millions of examples for the Hirsch conjecture and related problems, and over a million 5-dimensional prismatoids of width 6. The paper's own term is 'AI system'. It is not applied to uniform polytopes in the text I read.
systems.basis_quote: We present an Artificial Intelligence system capable of generating novel polytopes with very high complexity

events.what_happened: Richard Klitzing's version log on bendwavy.org, entry dated 2025/8/31: 'largely expanding on polytera', 'more than 50 new files within incmats and dimensional categories', 'more than 700 new incidence matrices'. It is a catalogue expansion with no new named convex 5-polytope and no completeness claim. Later entries (2026/2/2 and 2026/3/13) concern non-convex polychora and a 'mutesseract', with nothing on 5-dimensional convex members.
events.delivers: Catalogue growth of uniform polytera (incidence matrices). Makes no mathematical claim about the convex list.
events.doubts: Catalogue entries are not refereed. The polytera page says its non-convex list 'in fact just contains the so far provided polytera', and it does not claim completeness.
events.direction: No direction on the convex question; catalogue growth only.

events.what_happened: An edit to the Wikipedia 'Uniform 5-polytope' article on 6 April 2024 (user Double sharp, 15:02, per the history page as fetched) adds to the History of discovery: 'one more was discovered (snub cellibiprismatoteron, contains snub cubes as elements!)'. It is the only edit in the 2024-2026 history that changes the count of known 5-polytopes. I could not identify the polytope: four name searches and the Polytope Wiki snub pages turned up nothing that defines it, names a discoverer, says whether it is convex, or gives a first posting date. The edit has no footnote that I could see.
events.revisions: Wikipedia edit 6 Apr 2024 15:02 (count-changing); the same history shows other edits in 2024 and 2026 that do not change counts.
events.delivers: Unknown. If the claim is right, one more uniform 5-polytope is added to the article's total count, which mixes convex and non-convex members. Whether it is convex, and so a member of the convex list, is not established by anything I found.
events.remains: The whole problem, as far as I could establish.
events.time_since_posted: about 30 months (date of the Wikipedia edit, not of any first posting)
events.doubts: The edit is unsourced in what I saw, and the polytope cannot be found. The name suggests a prism-type product containing snub cubes; a search summary reports a 5-dimensional uniform 'scab' containing snub cubes, which I could not verify and cannot link to this name. Its first public posting may be earlier than the Wikipedia edit.
events.direction: Unknown. As written it is a count increase, with no stated direction relative to the convex question.

events.what_happened: Suvrit Sra, 'GPT, the Counterexample Machine', arXiv:2608.29595 (v1, 30 August 2026; math.CO, math.CA, math.FA). The abstract reports over 15 counterexamples in combinatorics, number theory, convexity and analysis, found with GPT Pro over 12 months. It contains no polytope, uniform, Wythoff or dimension-5 content; the full text was not read.
events.delivers: Counterexamples to unrelated conjectures, as the abstract describes them. Nothing on uniform 5-polytopes in the abstract.
events.direction: Different problems; cuts neither way on the convex 5-polytope question.

systems.name: GPT Pro
systems.what_it_did: Found more than 15 counterexamples across several areas, according to the abstract. None concerns uniform polytopes as far as the abstract shows.
systems.basis_quote: using GPT Pro over the course of 12 months

disputes.summary: Symmetry group of the 4D grand antiprism: Coxeter's [[10,2+,10]] (repeated in older Wikipedia mirrors) against Monson's +/-[D10 x D10].2, also of order 400. Monson says the Coxeter description is wrong and has propagated; a search summary says the current Wikipedia infobox uses Monson's group, which I did not verify on the live page. This bears on the 4D member and on the 5-dimensional grand antiprism prism that inherits it.

Who established completeness of the convex uniform 4-polytope list. Johnson's site (roice3) and Wikipedia-derived pages say Conway and Guy completed it by computer in 1965; other secondary sources credit Moller's 2004 dissertation with the completeness proof. The sources do not agree whether 1965 was a proof or a computation later proved complete. The Moller text was not opened.

Known-member counts disagree and mix scopes. Wikipedia (current, fetched) gives 104 known convex uniform 5-polytopes plus infinite families, and 1333 known uniform 5-polytopes outside infinite families, convex and non-convex together. The Open Problem Garden (2012) gives two infinite families plus 105 additional examples. The Polytope Wiki gives 1348 uniform polytera excluding prismatics (page edited 21 November 2025), and its list gives 1,350. Older mirrors give 1297. These are not reconciled, and the 2024 Wikipedia edit adds one more without a stated convexity.

summary: Convex uniform 5-polytopes are still listed as undetermined. The current Wikipedia article (fetched) says the complete set 'has not been determined', and its unsolved-problem box asks 'What is the complete set of convex uniform 5-polytopes?'. The Polytope Wiki (edited 21 November 2025) says it is not even known whether the convex list is complete. I found no source dated 26 January 2024 or later that enumerates, classifies or proves complete the convex 5-dimensional list, and no primary paper on it in the window: an arXiv keyword sweep for 'Wythoff uniform polytope' returns only Whitehead's 2020 regular-polytope paper, and a newest-first sweep for 'uniform polytopes' (247 hits, 43 read) shows nothing on uniform 5-polytopes. The in-window events I found are: (a) a Wikipedia edit of 6 April 2024 adding 'one more' discovered polytope ('snub cellibiprismatoteron') to the count, which I could not identify, so whether it is a convex member, and whether it was first posted in the window, are both unresolved; (b) Klitzing's catalogue expansions of polytera (31 August 2025 and later), which are catalogue work with no completeness or convex claim; and (c) arXiv papers on neighbouring questions: Monson 2024 (the 4D grand antiprism's symmetry group; preprint and journal both unreadable here), Martelli 2026 (Coxeter polyhedra, read in part), Schulte and Skacel 2026 (3D skeletal polyhedra), Swirszcz et al. 2025 (an AI search, 'Hopper', for polytopes in the Hirsch conjecture problem, not uniform polytopes) and Sra 2026 (GPT counterexamples with no polytope content). None of (c) is about this problem as stated. The pre-window record is substantial but partial: Schlafli (regular 5-polytopes: three, published 1901); Gosset 1900 (the semiregular list, including the 5-dimensional demipenteract); Coxeter 1940 to 1988 (a Wythoffian search); Johnson 1966 (two non-convex 5D antiprisms only); Conway and Guy 1965/1967 (the 4D convex list by computer, which contains the grand antiprism, whose 5D prism is the one known non-Wythoffian convex 5-member); Blind and Blind 1991 (completeness of the semiregular list, which covers the demipenteract); and Moller 2004 (a claimed 4D completeness proof, not opened). Together these settle the regular and semiregular subclasses and identify the Wythoffian and prismatic families, but nothing I opened closes the completeness of the full convex 5-dimensional list. On the AI question: no source I found credits any AI system with a convex uniform 5-polytope, and the 2024 Wikipedia addition names no system. The AI-related polytope work (Swirszcz et al. 2025) concerns other problems, and I have recorded it with that scope. Silence: the 2012 Open Problem Garden entry, the current Wikipedia article and the Polytope Wiki say substantively the same thing, so the 'open' status has held since at least 2012, and no later paper calls the list open or cites the earlier status, because no later paper on the list was found at all. Close calls: (1) the 2024 Wikipedia edit could be a convex member, which would turn the window's only event into a 'member added' event rather than nothing; (2) the 1901 date for Schlafli is the full publication, and earlier partial publications may carry the 5-dimensional material; (3) the 1940-1988 Coxeter series may have been meant as exhaustive in dimension 5, but the sources I read say it is not known to be complete, so I read it as not exhaustive.
competing_reading: The problem can be read as already classified in substance: Schlafli (regular, 1901), Gosset with Blind and Blind (semiregular, 1991), and the Coxeter and Johnson Wythoffian enumeration (1940-1966) cover most of the known members, and the only remaining gap is whether there are members beyond the Wythoffian families and the grand antiprism prism. On that reading the 'open' status reflects a completeness gap no one has tried to close, not an active open question, and the 2012 and 2026 statements are equally true. A second reading takes the 6 April 2024 Wikipedia addition at face value: if it is a convex member, the count moved inside the window, and the problem is an in-window 'moved a count' case rather than 'nothing happened'.
what_would_settle_it: (1) The text of Coxeter's Regular and Semi-Regular Polytopes I-III and of Johnson's 1991 Uniform Polytopes manuscript, chapters on dimension 5 (the roice3 page says its contents are 'coming'), to see whether either claims an exhaustive dimension-5 enumeration. (2) The footnote and definition behind the 6 April 2024 Wikipedia line, the polytope it names (a Klitzing acronym or a Polytope Wiki page), its convexity, and its first public posting date. (3) The primary text of Blind and Blind (1991), to confirm its dimension range and whether it says anything beyond the semiregular class. (4) The edit history of the convex count (104 in Wikipedia; 105 in the 2012 Open Problem Garden entry) to see whether a member was added and when. (5) An arXiv or journal paper dated after 26 January 2024 that enumerates or proves complete the convex 5-dimensional list; none turned up in 40-plus searches and arXiv keyword sweeps.
